title: MCP Goes Stateless: The 2026-07-28 Specification
content:
## Overview

The Model Context Protocol's next major specification, dated **2026-07-28**, makes a fundamental architectural change: MCP becomes **stateless at the protocol layer**. The release candidate locked on May 21, 2026, and the final spec ships July 28, 2026 — see the Tool Use & Agents page for background on what MCP is and why it exists.

---

## The Stateless Change

Prior MCP versions exchanged protocol version, client info, and capabilities once at connection time, then tracked a session via an `Mcp-Session-Id` header. That meant a client's requests had to keep landing on the same server instance — horizontal deployments needed sticky routing and shared session stores to work correctly.

2026-07-28 removes the protocol-level session entirely:

- Protocol version, client info, and capabilities now travel in `_meta` on **every request**, not just at connection
- A new `server/discover` method lets clients fetch server capabilities up front, whenever they need them
- The `Mcp-Session-Id` header is gone — any request can land on any server instance
- Result: MCP now runs on commodity HTTP infrastructure without sticky routing, which matters for anyone running MCP servers behind a standard load balancer rather than a single persistent process

---

## Extensions Framework

Rather than growing the core spec indefinitely, 2026-07-28 introduces an **extensions framework**: capabilities that used to require a full spec revision can now ship on their own timeline as opt-in extensions the client advertises support for.

### MCP Apps (SEP-1865)
Lets servers ship interactive HTML interfaces that hosts render inside a sandboxed iframe. Tools declare their UI templates ahead of time so hosts can prefetch, cache, and security-review them before anything executes. Every UI-initiated action still routes through the same JSON-RPC audit/consent path as a direct tool call — the interactive surface doesn't bypass permission checks.

### Tasks Extension
Tasks first shipped as an experimental **core** feature in the 2025-11-25 spec. Production use surfaced enough needed redesign that Anthropic and the MCP steering group moved it to an extension instead of baking it into core. Under the stateless model, a server can respond to `tools/call` with a task handle, and the client drives progress with `tasks/get`, `tasks/update`, and `tasks/cancel`. Task creation is server-directed — the client advertises support for the extension, but the server decides whether a given call should run as a background task.

---

## Enterprise Auth

Alongside the stateless core, MCP added centralized authorization support aimed at enterprise deployments — letting organizations manage access to many MCP servers through a single auth boundary rather than configuring credentials server-by-server. This lands as part of the same 2026 protocol evolution, addressing what had been one of the most commonly cited "growing pains" for production MCP use.

---

## Why This Matters

- **For server authors:** a stateless server is simpler to scale and deploy; existing session-based servers will need a migration path before the old session mechanics are formally deprecated
- **For client/host authors (like Claude Code):** capability discovery via `server/discover` and per-request `_meta` mean a client no longer has to assume a long-lived connection to a single server process
- **For the ecosystem:** the extensions framework is a bet that MCP's core should stay small and stable while higher-level capabilities (interactive UI, long-running tasks, enterprise auth) iterate independently — the same server surface that GitHub, Slack, and now X (which shipped a hosted MCP server on June 30, 2026) all build against

The practical migration window is May 21 – July 28, 2026: implementers building against the release candidate today should expect what they ship to keep working once the spec is finalized.
